content.text: high single oral doses cause GI irritation, so deficits are usually replaced in divided doses; a 1 mEq/L ↓K ≈ a 200 to 400 mEq total deficit, replaced over several days at 20 to 80 mEq/day.
arrhythmia: central vein, max 40 mEq/h, only w continuous cardiac monitoring; routine IV ≤ 10 mEq/h; avoid dextrose diluents (insulin can transiently worsen hypokalemia).

Tx of K depletion: 40 to 100 mEq/day or more. Prevention of hypokalemia: typically 20 mEq/day. Divide dosage if more than 20 mEq/day is given so no more than 20 mEq in a single dose. Take w/ meals and a glass of water; ⍉ on an empty stomach (potential for gastric irritation).

CI: hyperkalemia (further ↑ serum K can produce cardiac arrest). CI: any structural, pathological, or pharmacologic cause for arrest or delay in tablet passage through the GI tract. In pts w/ impaired K excretion, potassium salts can produce hyperkalemia and cardiac arrest; potentially fatal hyperkalemia can develop rapidly and be asymptomatic. ⍉ treat hypokalemia w/ concomitant potassium salts and a potassium-sparing diuretic (e.g., spironolactone, triamterene, or amiloride): severe hyperkalemia. Closely monitor K w/ concomitant RAAS therapy (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, eplerenone, or aliskiren). Closely monitor K w/ concomitant NSAID therapy. Discontinue immediately and consider ulceration, obstruction, or perforation if severe vomiting, abdominal pain, distention, or GI bleeding occurs. Careful monitoring of serum K and appropriate dosage adjustment required in chronic renal disease or any condition impairing K excretion. OD: hyperkalemia is usually asymptomatic and may be manifested only by an ↑ serum K (6.5 to 8 mEq/L) and ECG changes (peaking T-waves, loss of P-waves, S-T depression, QT prolongation). OD tx: IV calcium gluconate if the pt is at no risk or low risk of developing digitalis toxicity.
